title: Inequalities
intro: When an exact probability is out of reach, an inequality can still bound it. From Markov's one-line bound to Hoeffding's exponential one, these are the workhorses of proofs and of practical guarantees.

blocks.tex: P(X\ge a)\le\frac{E[X]}{a} \quad (X\ge0,\ a > 0), \qquad P(\vert X - \mu\vert\ge k)\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{k^2}

blocks.text: Markov's inequality uses only the mean: a non-negative variable cannot often be much larger than its average. Chebyshev's applies Markov to $(X - \mu)^2$ and uses the variance; it proves the weak law of large numbers in one line. Both are tight for some distributions, but usually very loose.
Applying Markov to $e^{tX}$ and optimising over $t$ gives the Chernoff bound, $P(X\ge a)\le\inf_{t>0}e^{-ta}M_X(t)$. For sums of independent bounded variables this yields Hoeffding's inequality:

blocks.caption: Hoeffding (1963). The same bound holds for the lower tail.

blocks.text: The difference from Chebyshev is the shape: Chebyshev decays like $1/n$, Hoeffding like $e^{-cn}$. That is what makes sample-size guarantees practical, and it is the basis of concentration of measure, PAC learning bounds, and the Hoeffding-plus-union-bound shot count on the QRC shelf's Measurement (#/qrc/open-systems/measurement) page.

items: Jensen: for convex $g$, $g(E[X])\le E[g(X)]$; for concave $g$ the inequality reverses. It gives $(E X)^2\le E[X^2]$, $E[\ln X]\le\ln E[X]$, the non-negativity of KL divergence, and the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality.
Union bound: $P\left(\bigcup A_i\right)\le\sum P(A_i)$, which turns a bound for one event into a bound for many.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
# Tail of X ~ Binomial(100, 0.5) above 70: exact vs Markov, Chebyshev, Chernoff/Hoeffding
n, p, a = 100, 0.5, 70
exact = stats.binom.sf(a - 1, n, p)
markov = n * p / a
cheb = n * p * (1 - p) / (a - n * p) ** 2            # bounds P(|X - 50| >= 20), so also the one tail
hoeff = np.exp(-2 * (a - n * p) ** 2 / n)
print(f"P(X >= 70) exact {exact:.2e} | Markov {markov:.3f} | Chebyshev {cheb:.4f} | Hoeffding {hoeff:.2e}")
# Jensen: for convex g, g(E X) <= E g(X)
rng = np.random.default_rng(21)
x = rng.exponential(1, 10 ** 6)
print(f"Jensen, g(x) = x^2: (E X)^2 = {x.mean()**2:.3f} <= E[X^2] = {np.mean(x**2):.3f}")
print(f"Jensen, concave log: E[ln X] = {np.mean(np.log(x)):.4f} <= ln E[X] = {np.log(x.mean()):.4f}  (E[ln X] = -0.5772, minus Euler's constant)")
# Cauchy-Schwarz: |Cov(X,Y)| <= sd(X) sd(Y)
y = x + rng.normal(size=10 ** 6)
print(f"|Cov| = {abs(np.cov(x, y)[0, 1]):.4f} <= sd sd = {x.std() * y.std():.4f}")

blocks.text: Output of the run: for $X\sim$ Binomial(100, 1/2), the exact $P(X\ge70) = 3.9\times10^{-5}$. Markov gives 0.714, Chebyshev 0.0625 and Hoeffding $3.4\times10^{-4}$: only the exponential bound is in the right neighbourhood. Jensen holds in both directions tested ($1.004\le2.008$; $E[\ln X] = -0.575\le\ln E[X] = 0.002$), and Cauchy–Schwarz gives $1.00\le1.42$.

blocks.title: Markov for a waiting time
blocks.text: A queue has mean waiting time 2 minutes. Bound the probability of waiting at least 10 minutes. What if the standard deviation is also known to be 1 minute?

blocks.title: How many samples for a polling guarantee
blocks.text: How many independent yes/no responses guarantee, by Hoeffding, that the sample proportion is within 0.01 of the truth with probability at least 0.95?

blocks.title: Jensen and the AM–GM inequality
blocks.text: Use Jensen with $g = -\ln$ to show $(x_1x_2\cdots x_n)^{1/n}\le(x_1 + \cdots + x_n)/n$ for positive $x_i$.
solution: Let $X$ be uniform on $\{x_1, \dots, x_n\}$. $\ln$ is concave, so $E[\ln X]\le\ln E[X]$.
